summary.text: Resonance is a way of describing bonding in some molecules or ions by combining several contributing structures into a resonance hybrid.
It is valuable for delocalized electrons, where the bonding cannot be expressed by one single Lewis structure.
The hybrid is an average of the contributing structures, not a molecule that shifts back and forth between them.

facts.label: First appeared
facts.value: 1899, in Johannes Thiele's Partial Valence Hypothesis

items.prompt: The two N–O bonds in the nitrite ion measure the same length, yet any single drawing shows one single and one double bond. How is this reconciled?

options.label: One bond is single and the other double, and they swap places too fast to measure
The measurement is wrong, because bonds in one ion cannot be equal
The real ion is an average of the drawings, so each bond is in between
The ion is really two different species mixed together

items.explain: Each N–O bond is an average of a formal single and a formal double bond, giving a true bond order of 1.5 and equal bonds.

items.prompt: A friend says a molecule drawn as a resonance hybrid keeps flipping rapidly between its different drawings. What is the best reply?

options.label: No, it has one well-defined geometry and electron distribution that is an average
Yes, the electrons shift back and forth between the drawings
Yes, but only when the molecule is heated
No, the molecule actually matches only its single lowest-energy drawing

items.explain: A resonance hybrid does not mean electrons are resonating between sets of positions. It means the structures represent an intermediate structure with a single, well-defined geometry.

items.prompt: Two drawings of a molecule differ only in how electrons are assigned to atoms, with the atoms in the same places. Are they isomers?

options.label: Yes, any two different drawings of a molecule are isomers
Yes, because the electron assignments differ between them
No, because isomers must have different chemical formulas
No, they are contributors to one species; isomers arrange atoms differently

items.explain: Isomers are distinct chemical species with different arrangements of atomic nuclei, while resonance contributors differ only in how electrons are formally assigned.

items.prompt: Compared with any one of the hypothetical drawings, how stable is the real species described by a resonance hybrid?

options.label: Less stable, since averaging blurs the structure
More stable, since delocalizing electrons lowers its energy
Equally stable, since the drawings describe the same species
More stable, since resonance adds extra electrons to it

items.explain: Electron delocalization lowers the potential energy of a system, so a species represented by a resonance hybrid is more stable than any of its hypothetical contributing structures.

items.prompt: Kekulé's alternating-bond picture of benzene predicts four dibromobenzene isomers. What is found in reality, and what does it suggest?

options.label: Four exist, as predicted, showing the alternating bonds are real
Three exist, showing the double bonds sit in fixed positions
Only one exists, showing benzene has no bonds between carbons
Only three exist, suggesting every carbon–carbon bond is the same intermediate kind

items.explain: Only three dibromobenzene isomers exist, and only one is ortho, in agreement with a single type of carbon-carbon bond intermediate between single and double.

items.prompt: A student draws two contributing structures for one ion, but one drawing shows two more valence electrons than the other. What is wrong?

options.label: Contributors must all account for the same number of valence electrons
Nothing, since contributors may differ freely in electron number
Contributors must have different formal charges on every atom
The drawings need a double-headed arrow replaced by an equilibrium arrow

items.explain: Contributing structures may differ in bond orders and formal charges, but all must have the same number of valence electrons and the same spin multiplicity.

paragraphs.heading: Many drawings, one molecule
paragraphs.text: Resonance, also called mesomerism, describes the bonding in certain molecules or polyatomic ions by combining several contributing structures into one resonance hybrid. It belongs to valence bond theory and is used when no single Lewis structure can capture the bonding. It is especially valuable when electrons are delocalized. The hybrid is the accurate structure, an average of the contributing structures, which are only hypothetical.

paragraphs.heading: Why it is needed
paragraphs.text: For many substances, one Lewis structure, with atoms obeying the octet rule and bonds of whole-number order, explains measured features such as bond lengths, angles and dipole moment. Sometimes, though, more than one structure can be drawn, and the measurements fit none of them. Chemists then treat several contributing structures together as an average and call the result a resonance hybrid.

paragraphs.heading: The nitrite example
paragraphs.text: In the nitrite ion, NO₂^(–), both N–O bonds have the same length, yet no single Lewis structure gives them the same bond order. Both measure 125 pm, between a typical N–O single bond at 145 pm and an N–O double bond at 115 pm. Averaging the two contributing structures makes each bond halfway between single and double, a bond order of 1.5. That squares the drawing with the measured fact that the two bonds are equivalent.

paragraphs.heading: Lower energy
paragraphs.text: Spreading electrons out lowers the potential energy of a system, so any species described by a resonance hybrid is steadier than each of its contributing structures. With the electrons spread more evenly over the molecule, they repel each other less. The energy gap between the real species and the lowest-energy contributing structure is called the resonance energy or delocalization energy. Its size depends on the assumptions and methods used, and it is not a quantity that can be measured.

paragraphs.heading: Not flipping back and forth
paragraphs.text: Resonance is different from isomerism. Isomers share a formula but are distinct substances with their atoms arranged differently in space, while resonance contributors differ only in how electrons are assigned to atoms on paper. A hybrid does not mean electrons shift back and forth between positions; it is one structure with a single well-defined geometry and electron distribution. A narwhal makes a good comparison: it can be described as part unicorn, with one horn, and part leviathan, a large whale-like creature. It never switches between the two, and neither of them exists outside the imagination, yet the description still fits it well.

paragraphs.heading: How it is drawn
paragraphs.text: Contributing structures are usually separated by double-headed arrows (↔), which should not be confused with the equilibrium arrow (⇌). The whole set may be enclosed in large square brackets to show it pictures one molecule or ion. In a hybrid structure, pi bonds taking part in resonance are drawn as curves or dashed lines. In benzene and other aromatic rings, a solid circle is sometimes drawn to show the delocalized pi electrons.

paragraphs.heading: Benzene's puzzle
paragraphs.text: The idea was first put forward in 1899, in the Partial Valence Hypothesis of Johannes Thiele. It was meant to explain why benzene was more stable than August Kekulé's 1865 structure, with alternating single and double bonds, would lead one to expect. Thiele proposed that each carbon-carbon bond in benzene sits between a single and a double bond. This also explained isomer counts: Kekulé's structure predicts four dibromobenzene isomers, but in reality there are three, and only one of them is ortho.
